blocks.md: You already know 하다 → **해요**. The payoff is bigger than one verb: **a huge share of Korean verbs are just a noun with 하다 stuck on the end.**
This means **every new 하다 noun you learn is a free verb.** Learn the noun 청소 (cleaning) and you can immediately say 청소해요. No conjugation to work out — the 하다 half always becomes 해요.

items.tip: I study at the cafe. Note 에서 — studying is an action.

blocks.q: “I cook at home.”
blocks.why: 요리하다 is an action so the place takes **에서**, and 하다 becomes **해요**. 요리하요 is the mistake of conjugating 하다 regularly — it never does that. 요리에요 confuses the noun ending 이에요/예요 with a verb.
하다 always turns into **해요**. 일하요 applies the regular rule, which 하다 refuses. 일이에요 means “it is work” — a noun sentence, not an action.

blocks.q: “I study every day.”  저는 매일 ___

blocks.why: 전화 + 하다 → **전화해요**. 전화하요 conjugates 하다 regularly, which it never does; 전화예요 and 전화이에요 are noun endings meaning “it is a phone call”.

blocks.q: You learn a new noun: 청소 (cleaning). How do you say “I clean”?
blocks.why: Any 하다 noun becomes a verb for free — 청소**해요**. That is the payoff of this pattern: every new 하다 noun is a new verb you can already conjugate.

blocks.q: Build “I exercise every day.”
Write it yourself: **“I study at the cafe.”**  (cafe = 카페)
blocks.hint: Studying is an action — so 에 or 에서? And 공부하다 becomes what?
blocks.why: 카페에서 공부해요. Two things at once here: the action place takes 에서, and 하다 always becomes 해요.

blocks.q: Say it out loud: “I exercise every day.”

blocks.md:
Here is something English speakers find hard to believe at first.

커피 마셔요.

That one sentence can mean **three different things**, and nothing in the writing tells you which. Only the voice does.

**Korean does not reorder words to ask a question.** English flips *you are* into *are you*. Korean leaves the sentence exactly as it is and lifts the end of it. This is why Korean questions feel so easy once you notice it — there is nothing extra to learn.

items.tip: Falling: “I eat with them.” Bright and toward someone: “Let’s eat together.”
Where are you going? — rising at the end.
Statement, or the everyday way to say “See you tomorrow.”

blocks.q: Your friend says “주말에 영화 봐요!” warmly while looking at you. What is it?
options: An invitation — let’s watch a movie
A statement about their own weekend
A command telling you to watch
blocks.why: Said brightly toward you, the plain 해요 form is the everyday way to suggest doing something together. Falling and about themselves it would be a statement; rising it would be a question. A direct command would normally use **-(으)세요** — 보세요.
The invitation uses the same plain **먹어요**. With a question mark it becomes a question; 먹이에요 wrongly attaches the noun ending; 먹다 is the dictionary form, which is not used to speak to someone.

blocks.q: Build “Where are you going?”

blocks.meaning: (at a shop) How much is this?
blocks.why: 얼마 ends in a vowel → **얼마예요**, said with a rising end. 얼마이에요 uses the consonant form; 얼마해요 and 얼마있어요 attach verbs where the noun ending belongs.

blocks.q: Written down, 어디 가요 could be two things. Which two?
options: a statement and a past tense
blocks.why: Rising, it asks *where are you going*; falling, it states *I am going somewhere*. A command would normally use **-(으)세요** — 가세요.

blocks.q: Write it yourself: **“Where are you going?”**
blocks.hint: Korean does not reorder words to ask. Say it as a statement and let your voice do the asking.
blocks.why: 어디 가요? Both 어디 가요 and 어디에 가요 are natural; the 에 is often dropped in speech.

blocks.q: Say it out loud warmly as an invitation: “Let’s have coffee together!”

title.ko: 3강. 하다 동사 확장과 세 가지 쓰임
title.en: Lesson 3. Expanding 하다 Verbs and Three Uses

blocks.h: More Everyday 하다 Verbs in Action
blocks.md:
As you saw, any noun that describes an activity can pair with **하다** to become a verb.

All of them turn into **-해요** in polite speech. With just the tone of your voice or punctuation, you can make a **statement**, ask a **question**, or give an **invitation**!
Because these are all -하다 verbs, you don't need to check vowel harmony rules for them: every single one becomes **-해요**!

items.tip: I cook at home on the weekend. (Statement)
Are you taking a walk in the park now? (Question)
Let’s go shopping at the department store! (Invitation)

blocks.q: How do you conjugate ‘산책하다’ (to take a walk) into polite present form?
blocks.why: All verbs ending in -하다 conjugate to **-해요** in polite speech. 산책하요 and 산책아요 are incorrect forms.

blocks.q: Match each noun with its correct conjugated verb form.

blocks.meaning: I chat with a friend at a cafe today.
blocks.why: Present polite form of 이야기하다 is **이야기해요**. 이야기하요 is incorrect.

blocks.q: 요리하다 (to cook) — Complete the statement: 「저녁에 집에서 ___ .」
blocks.why: 요리하다 always conjugates to **요리해요** in polite speech.

blocks.q: Build the invitation: “Let’s walk together in the park!”
Say it out loud warmly as an invitation: “Let’s take a walk together with a friend this weekend!”

blocks.h: Telling the Three Roles Apart in Dialogue
blocks.md:
Because **해요** looks the same for statements, questions, and invitations, context and punctuation guide you in reading:

- **Question (?):** Rising tone at the very end.
- **Statement (.):** Steady or falling tone.
- **Invitation (!):** Said toward someone, often with words like **같이** (together) or **우리** (we / let's).
When someone asks **“지금 뭐 해요?”** (What are you doing?), reply with a statement ending in **-해요** or **-어요**, like **“책 읽어요”** or **“운동해요”**.

items.tip: Question: Are you studying now? (rising tone)
Statement answer: Yes, I am studying Korean now.

blocks.q: A friend asks: “오늘 저녁에 뭐 해요?” How should you naturally reply if you plan to exercise?
blocks.why: The friend asked a question. You answer with a statement ending with a period and a falling tone: **운동해요.**

blocks.q: You want to suggest to a coworker: “Let's start now!” Which sentence matches this mood best?
blocks.why: When making an enthusiastic suggestion or invitation to do something together, say **지금 시작해요!** with an inviting tone.

blocks.q: Match each dialogue line to its communicative intention.

blocks.sentence: A: 지금 어디 가요? B: 도서관에서 [공부해요].
blocks.meaning: A: Where are you going now? B: I'm studying at the library.
blocks.why: B is answering a question with a statement, so use **공부해요**.

blocks.q: Start an invitation using 시작하다: 「우리 이제 회의를 ___ !」
blocks.why: 시작하다 conjugates to **시작해요** for invitations as well as statements and questions.

blocks.say: A: 지금 뭐 해요? B: 공원에서 운동해요.
blocks.rom: A: ji-geum mwo hae-yo? B: gong-won-e-seo un-dong-hae-yo
blocks.q: Read both lines out loud, raising your voice for the question and lowering it for the statement.
Arrange the words to say: “What are you doing today?”
